summary: First English narrative for the 20 April 2010 decision on the Deepwater Horizon to accept the Macondo negative-pressure test despite an unresolved 1,400 psi drill-pipe reading, written from the case's verified facts (National Commission report to the President, January 2011; press coverage of the Chief Counsel's report). Field personnel are identified by role only.

narrative.hook: It is nearly 8 p.m. on a drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico. One gauge says the well is sealed; another, which should agree with it, has read 1,400 psi for half an hour. You are the company's supervisor, and you have to decide which one to believe.
narrative.short_setup: On 20 April 2010 the Deepwater Horizon is finishing BP's Macondo well, about 40 miles off the Louisiana coast, and preparing to leave it temporarily sealed. Before the heavy drilling mud is replaced with seawater, the crew runs a negative-pressure test: bleed the pressure in the well to zero, close it, and watch. If nothing flows and no pressure comes back, the cement at the bottom is holding back the reservoir. It is the only test planned that will check that cement. The well is almost six weeks behind schedule and more than $58 million over budget, and no regulation, industry protocol or company procedure says exactly how to run or read this test. BP's Well Site Leaders, the company's supervisors on the rig, make the call together with the drilling contractor Transocean's crew.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: The test exists to answer one question, and its own rule is simple: once the pressure is bled off and the pipe is closed, it must stay at zero. On the drill pipe it did not. Three times the crew bled it down, and three times it came back, finally to 1,400 psi. The kill line ran to the same place as the drill pipe and should have shown the same reading, so a clean result on one and 1,400 psi on the other was a contradiction, not a pass. At least one experienced member of the crew was, by one recollection, unconvinced by the explanations. Stopping would mean keeping the well shut in, calling shore for a second opinion, and testing again until the numbers made sense. If the cement had failed, this was the last moment to find out while the heavy mud was still holding the well.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: Proceeding was not reckless on its face. The repeat test on the kill line met the success criterion: after a little fluid flowed and stopped, there was no flow for 30 minutes. BP had told the regulator in its permit application that the test would be run on the kill line. An experienced toolpusher offered an explanation for the drill-pipe reading, a 'bladder effect' from the heavy mud pressing on the preventer, and, according to BP witnesses, said he had seen it before. The positive-pressure test that afternoon had held. There was no written procedure saying which line governed. And treating the result as a failure could mean days of diagnosis and repair on a well already far behind schedule.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: At 8 p.m. the BP Well Site Leaders, in consultation with the crew, concluded that the kill-line test had confirmed the integrity of the well, declared the negative-pressure test a success, and moved on. Two minutes later the crew opened the preventer and began replacing the mud and spacer in the riser with seawater. The two readings were never reconciled. By the commission's account, the Well Site Leaders did not consult anyone on shore about the anomalous data. The 'bladder effect' is recorded in post-incident statements; one witness said he did not recall anyone agreeing or disagreeing with it.
narrative.outcome_story: The cement had not held. As mud came out of the riser, hydrocarbons flowed up the well. By about 9:45 p.m. the rig was on fire: the well had blown out, and escaping gas had exploded. Eleven workers died and 16 injured crew members were evacuated. The rig sank on 22 April. By government estimates, more than 4 million barrels of oil spilled into the Gulf before the well was sealed months later. The presidential commission found that the pressure data had not been ambiguous: they showed repeatedly that fluids were flowing into the well, and the 1,400 psi reading could only have come from a leak. It also noted that the untested spacer may have clogged the kill line. It called the failure to conduct and interpret the test properly a major contributing factor to the blowout, alongside failures in cementing, in detecting the kick, and in responding to it. Industry experts consulted by the commission's lawyers dismissed the 'bladder effect' as a fiction.
narrative.hindsight_analysis:
The outcome was catastrophic, and it is tempting to grade the decision by that alone. The fairer question is what the people in the drill shack could see.

On decision quality, the choice rates as weak. The point is not that they should have known the cement had failed. It is that the test, on its own terms, had not passed. The drill pipe kept rebuilding pressure, the kill line should have matched it and did not, and the explanation offered was not checked against anything. The reasons for proceeding were real: one test passed, the permit named the kill line, an experienced colleague had an answer, nothing in writing said what to do, and delay was expensive. But each of those reasons explains why stopping felt hard. None of them explains the 1,400 psi. When the purpose of a check is to catch exactly this kind of signal, an unexplained signal should count against the pass, not be argued around.

On outcome quality, the result could hardly have been worse. But it was not the product of this decision alone. The commission traced the blowout through several failures: the cement job, the choice of spacer, the procedure for temporary abandonment, the missed signs of a kick in the following hour, and the response once it came. A correct reading of the test would very likely have stopped the sequence, but the blowout needed the later failures too. The system also set these supervisors up badly. There were no procedures for the test, no enforced rule to call shore, and concerns about the cement had not been passed to the rig. Lessons from a similar near-miss on a Transocean rig in the North Sea four months earlier had not reached this crew.

So two things are true at once. The decision was weak on the information at hand. And it was made inside an organisation that had left the people making it without the procedures, context and second opinions that would have made the right call easier.
narrative.decision_principle: When a safety check is designed to catch a specific danger, a reading that fails it should not be explained away by a second reading that passes; until the contradiction is resolved, treat the check as failed.
narrative.longform_story:
On the evening of 20 April 2010, the Deepwater Horizon was nearly done. The rig, owned by Transocean and working for BP, had drilled the Macondo well in the Gulf of Mexico, about 40 miles off Louisiana. It had found a large reservoir of oil and gas. What remained was to leave the well safely sealed until a production rig came to complete it. The well had been difficult. By then it was almost six weeks behind schedule and more than $58 million over budget.

Temporary abandonment meant replacing the heavy drilling mud in the well and the riser with much lighter seawater. That would take away pressure that had been holding the reservoir in check. Before doing it, the crew had to be sure the cement at the bottom of the well would hold on its own. The test for that is called a negative-pressure test. The crew bleeds the pressure inside the well down to zero, closes it, and watches. If nothing flows and the pressure stays at zero, the cement is sealing. At Macondo it was the only test planned that would check that cement.

The positive-pressure test, which checks the casing by pumping pressure in, had passed at noon. The negative test began at 5 p.m. It did not go cleanly. On the drill pipe, the crew could not at first bleed the pressure below 266 psi, and when they closed it, it jumped to 1,262 psi. Fluid had been leaking past a preventer at the seabed; that was fixed. They bled the drill pipe to zero again, and when they closed it, the pressure came back to at least 773 psi. They did it a third time. It came back to 1,400 psi.

The shift was changing, and the drill shack was crowded. Both of BP's Well Site Leaders were there, along with both of Transocean's toolpushers and the driller. A group of visiting BP and Transocean executives passed through on a tour. In the discussion that followed, one of the toolpushers offered an explanation. The pressure, he said, was a 'bladder effect': the heavy mud above the preventer was pressing on it and pushing pressure into the drill pipe. According to BP witnesses, he said he had seen it before. One witness later said he did not recall anyone agreeing or disagreeing. The toolpusher going off shift, by one colleague's recollection, was convinced that something wasn't right.

One of the Well Site Leaders insisted on running the test again, this time on the kill line. The kill line is a separate pipe from the rig down to the blowout preventer, and BP had told the regulator it would use that line for the test. The kill line and the drill pipe led to the same place, so they should have shown the same pressure. On the kill line, a little fluid flowed and then stopped, and for 30 minutes there was no flow at all. By that measure the test passed. But all that time the drill pipe sat at 1,400 psi.

This was the moment of decision. Nothing in the regulations, in written industry practice, or in BP's or Transocean's own procedures said how to read a result like this. BP's onshore team had not sent specific instructions for this test, and there was no enforced rule to call shore for a second opinion on confusing data. The case for moving on was easy to state. One test had passed. The permit named the kill line. An experienced hand had an explanation. Stopping could mean days of work on a well that was already very late. The case for stopping was simpler still: a test meant to catch flow into the well had produced a reading that only made sense if there was flow, and no one had shown otherwise.

At 8 p.m. the Well Site Leaders, with the crew, declared the test a success. Two minutes later the crew opened the preventer and began pumping seawater in to push the mud and spacer out of the riser.

The cement had failed. As the mud came out, hydrocarbons moved up the well. Around 9:45 p.m., three men out tuna fishing saw a brilliant light on the horizon and heard a Mayday from the Deepwater Horizon. The well had blown out and gas had exploded on the rig. Eleven workers were killed. Sixteen injured crew members were flown to hospitals. The rig burned through the night and sank on 22 April. By government estimates, more than 4 million barrels of oil poured into the Gulf before the well was finally sealed months later.

The presidential commission that investigated the disaster was blunt about the test. It was undisputed, the commission wrote, that the test had been conducted and interpreted improperly. The data had not been ambiguous: they showed again and again that fluids were flowing into the well, and the 1,400 psi reading could only have been caused by a leak. The commission suggested that the unusual spacer BP had chosen, made from leftover materials and never tested for the job, may have clogged the kill line, producing the clean reading. The industry experts its lawyers consulted dismissed the 'bladder effect' as a fiction. It appeared, the commission wrote, that the men had started from the assumption that the well could not be flowing, and kept testing and explaining until they had convinced themselves.

The commission did not stop at the drill shack, though. It found that there was no standard procedure for the test anywhere: not in the regulations, not in industry protocols, and not inside BP or Transocean. Concerns about the cement job known onshore had largely not been passed to the rig. Transocean had not shared with its crews the lessons of a strikingly similar near-miss on one of its rigs in the North Sea four months earlier, where a barrier failed after a negative test had been declared a success. And the blowout itself needed more than one mistake: the cement had to fail, the signs of the kick in the following hour had to be missed, and the response had to fall short.

How should the decision itself be judged? The people in the shack could not see the cement. They could see a test that had passed one way and failed another, and an explanation that nobody checked. The pressures to move on were real: time, money, a colleague's confidence, a permit that named the other line. But none of those pressures explained the number on the gauge. The decision was weak on what was in front of them. It was also made inside a system that gave them no procedure, no context and no habit of asking for help, and that is where much of the lesson lies.
